Asymmetric Construction of Chiral 2-Azetines and Axially Chiral
Tetrasubstituted Allenes Via Phosphine Catalysis
Yi Tang
+

+

Abstract: Chiral 2-azetines and allenes are highly
valuable structural units in natural products and useful
chemicals. However, enantioselective synthesis of both
2-azetines and allenes has been extremely challenging.
Herein, we present asymmetric construction of chiral 2-
azetines (70–98 % yields and up to 96 % ee) through
chiral phosphine-catalyzed [2 + 2] annulation of yne-
enones with sulfamate-derived cyclic imines. These 2-
azetines were easily transformed into chiral allenes upon
treatment with Et
3
SiH, BF
3
· Et
2
O and water at rt for
2 minutes. Based on the above transformations, a
concise one-pot synthetic procedure combining [2 + 2]
annulation of yne-enones and sulfamate-derived cyclic
imines under phosphine catalysis and sequential reduc-
tion/isomerization/ring-opening reaction through
Et
3
SiH, BF
3
· Et
2
O and water was thus set up, providing
axially chiral tetrasubstituted allenes in satisfactory
yields and enantioselectivities (56–90 % yields and up to
91 % ee).
A xially chiral allenes are valuable structural units in natural
products, bioactive molecules and pharmaceuticals.
[1]
Partic-
ularly, compounds containing both axial chirality and central
chirality such as chiral allenes bearing a vicinal chiral cycles
(Figure 1a) are getting more and more attention due to their
presence in numerous bioactive molecules. Therefore,
numerous efficient synthetic methods for chiral allenes have
been developed.
[2]
Among them, metal-catalyzed asymmetric
processes
[3]
and certain exquisite organocatalytic asymmetric
methods
[4]
displayed remarkable proficiency in the produc-
tion of chiral allenes. On the other hand, functionalized
four-membered azaheterocycles are also widely present in
bioactive molecules.
[5]
There are four types of four-mem-
bered azaheterocycles including azetidine and 2-azetidinone,
and their unsaturated analogues such as 1-azetine and 2-
azetine (Figure 1b). Significant progress has been made over
the past decades for the synthesis of azetidine and 2-
azetidinone.
[6]
In contrast, the synthesis of 1-azetine and 2-
azetine has been much less investigated
[7]
due to their
potential 4π-electrocyclic ring opening to the corresponding
more stable aza-1,3-butadienes.
[8]

of our knowledge, only one available method has been
reported for the synthesis of chiral 2-azetines (Scheme 1a).
[9]
For this reason, it is of great importance to establish simple
and efficient method to synthesize chiral 2-azetines and
axially chiral allenes.
As an important part of organocatalysis, phosphine-cata-
lyzed reactions have drawn great attention and become an
efficient tool for synthesis of valuable compounds in the past
two decades.
[10,11]
Synthesis of allenes under phosphine catalysis
are also achievable.
[12]
However, to the best of our knowledge,
only one kinetic resolution process of racemic γ-substituted
allenoates through chiral phosphine was developed for the
preparation of axially chiral allenoates (up to 85 % ee)
(Scheme 1b).
[12a]
In this context, we anticipated to develop a
new tool via phosphine catalysis for synthesis of chiral 2-azetines
and axially chiral allenes. Due to particular reactivity, yne-
enones showed enormous potential as versatile building blocks
for synthesis of acyclic and cyclic compounds under transition
metal catalysis (Pd, Au, Rh, etc.)
[13]
and organocatalysis (NR
3
,
PR
3
).
[14]
Surprisingly, application of yne-enones in phosphine
catalysis was very limited.
[14f,g]

lective synthesis of stable chiral 2-azetines and axially chiral
tetrasubstituted allenes via phosphine-catalyzed [2 + 2] annula-
tion of yne-enones with sulfamate-derived cyclic imines (Sche-
me 1c).

Under the optimal reaction conditions, the substrate scope
of asymmetric [2 + 2] annulation was examined. As shown in
Scheme 2, the reactions of yne-enones 1 a–1 p with sulfamate-
derived cyclic imine 2 a proceeded smoothly to give the products
3 aa–3 pa in 70–98 % yields with 56–96 % ee. Generally, varia-
tion of substituent R
2
in acyl group did not influence reactivity
of yne-enones. The enantioselectivity of product 3 ca decreased
a lot when R
2
in acyl group was phenyl. Unfortunately, when R
2
was ethoxyl, the reaction did not occur under standard reaction
conditions. In addition, the substrates having electron-deficient
substituents on the aryl ring R
1

enantioselectivities to that of those substrates bearing electron-
rich substituents. Strong electron-withdrawing cyano and CF
3
group were also well tolerated, affording the products 3 ja and
3 ka in high yields, albeit with slightly lower enantioselectivities.
In particular, when the substituent R
1
on the alkynyl moiety was
2-naphthyl or 2-thienyl, the corresponding product 3 oa or 3 pa
was obtained in high yield with excellent enantioselectivity. It
was regrettable that when R
1
group on the alkynyl moiety was
H, alkyl or trimethylsilyl (TMS), the reaction did not work.
Under phosphine catalysis, TMS-substituted substrate might
underwent desilylation, thus leading to messy mixture. As for
tert-butyl-substituted yne-enone 1 s or the yne-enone 1 r without
substituent, it was difficult to form allenyl anion intermediate.
We further explored this annulation reaction of various
sulfamate-derived cyclic imines 2. As shown in Scheme 3,
various easily synthesized cyclic imines 2 b–2 n reacted smoothly
with yne-enone 1 d, affording the corresponding products 3 db–
3 dn in high yields with moderate to excellent enantioselectivities
(83–98 % yields, 48–91 % ee). It is worth noting that the cyclic
imines 2 having substituent at 8-position afforded products in
higher enantioselectivities, compared with those cyclic imines
bearing substituent at 6-position or 5-position (3 dd vs 3 df, 3 dm
vs 3 dn). Therefore, we additionally used 1 b to react with two
cyclic imines 2 c and 2 g having substituent at 8-position, giving
the corresponding product 3 bc and 3 bg in 89 % and 77 % yields
with 91 % and 90 % ee, respectively. The structure and stereo-
chemistry of 3 bc (CCDC Number: 2340414, detailed in SI) were
determined through single-crystal X-ray diffraction.
[15]
After asymmetric [2 + 2] annulation of yne-enones 1 with
sulfamate-derived cyclic imines 2 was investigated, we explored
asymmetric construction of axially chiral tetrasubstituted allenes.

As shown in Scheme 4, several yne-enones 1 were examined
under the optimized one-pot reaction conditions, giving the
corresponding allene products 4 in 56–90 % yields with
moderate to high diastereo- and enantioselectivities (6 : 1 to
> 20 : 1 dr, 62–91 % ee). In general, the yne-enones having
electron-deficient substituents on the aryl ring showed similar
reactivity to that of those substrates bearing electron-rich
substituents. In addition, the strong electron-withdrawing CF
3
group was well tolerated, resulting in 72 % yield of product 4 ka,
albeit with somewhat deteriorative enantioselectivity (62 % ee).
When the substituent on the alkynyl moiety was 2-naphthyl or
2-thienyl, the corresponding allene products 4 oa and 4 pa were
also obtained in 70 % and 72 % yields with 90 % and 89 % ee,
respectively. We then moved on to evaluate the scope of cyclic
imines 2. Several cyclic imines having different substituents were
examined with yne-enone 1 a, 1 b or 1 d as the reaction partner
and the desired products 4 were obtained in 61–90 % yields with
80–91 % ee and 6 : 1 to > 20 : 1 dr. The cyclic imines 2 bearing
electron-donating groups such as 8-OEt, 8-Me, 8-OMe, 8-t-Bu
and 7-i-Pr and electron-withdrawing groups such as 6-F all
delivered the desired products (4 ab, 4 ad, 4 bc, 4 bg, 4 dh, 4 aj
and 4 dj) in high yields with good enantio- and diastereoselectiv-
ities. The absolute configurations of the products were
determined by X-ray crystallographic analysis of the product
3 bc and rac-4 da (CCDC Number: 2351222, detailed in SI).
[15]
Furthermore, the scale-up preparations of the products 3 da
and 4 da were carried out. As indicated in Scheme 5a, 1.0 mmol
(183 mg) of the sulfamate-derived cyclic imine 2 a was reacted
with the yne-enone 1 d under the optimal reaction conditions to
give the product 3 da in 89 % yield with 91 % ee and product
4 da in 50 % yield with 90 % ee and > 20 : 1 dr, respectively.

We also tried other electron-deficient imines such as cyclic
imines 10 and 11, isatin-derived ketoimine 12 and N-sulfonyl
imines 13 and 14 (Scheme 6). Either no reaction occurred or the
corresponding aza-1,3-butadienes 15 and 16 were formed via the
4π-electrocyclic ring opening. These results indicated that highly
electron-deficient property and ring size of cyclic imine were
crucial for the current annulation.
As depicted in Scheme 7, a plausible mechanism was
proposed. Nucleophilic addition of phosphine catalyst to yne-
enone 1 a afforded the zwitterionic intermediate A, which
isomerized to generate the allenyl anion intermediate C. The
intermediate C then attacked the sulfamate-derived cyclic imine
2 a from the Re face to give the intermediate D. Subsequent
intramolecular annulation yielded the intermediate E. The chiral
2-azetine product 3 aa was then produced through β-elimination
of the phosphine. In the one-pot reaction procedure, Lewis acid
BF
3
activated the carbonyl group of 3 aa. Subsequently,
sequential reduction/rearrangement/ring-opening reaction
through Et
3
SiH occurred to give the intermediate G, which was
hydrolysed to produce the allene product 4 aa.
To gain further insight into the stereoselectivity of the
current reaction, we performed theoretical calculations. The
calculated free energy profiles were shown in Figure 2. The
conversion of substrate 2 a into the intermediate D generated a
chiral center and a chiral axis, therefore four possible reaction
pathways were discussed for the reaction of 2 a and the
intermediate A. The Re-S pathway (Figure 2, black) was
identified as the more favourable reaction pathway in view of its
relatively lower reaction energy barrier (7.87 kcal/mol) than the
other three competing pathways. This can be attributed to the
weaker steric hindrance in the transition state structure C-ts in

In conclusion, we have achieved asymmetric construction of
chiral 2-azetines and axially chiral tetrasubstituted allenes in
moderate to high yields with good to excellent stereoselectivities
through phosphine catalysis. Chiral phosphine-catalyzed [2 + 2]
annulation of sulfamate-derived cyclic imines with yne-enones
produced enantioenriched 2-azetine derivatives, which was
treated with Et
3

3
· Et

2

procedure to give axially chiral tetrasubstituted allenes. This
new application of yne-enones in phosphine catalysis will inspire
more exploration on yne-enones as a versatile acceptor for
phosphine-catalysed reactions.

imines under phosphine catalysis and sequential reduc-

Et SiH,

We also tried other electron-deficient imines such as cyclic
imines 10 and 11, isatin-derived ketoimine 12 and N-sulfonyl
imines 13 and 14 (Scheme 6). Either no reaction occurred or the
corresponding aza-1,3-butadienes 15 and 16 were formed via the
4π-electrocyclic ring opening. These results indicated that highly
electron-deficient property and ring size of cyclic imine were
crucial for the current annulation.

As depicted in Scheme 7, a plausible mechanism was
proposed. Nucleophilic addition of phosphine catalyst to yne-
enone 1a afforded the zwitterionic intermediate A, which
isomerized to generate the allenyl anion intermediate C. The
intermediate C then attacked the sulfamate-derived cyclic imine
2a from the Re face to give the intermediate D. Subsequent
intramolecular annulation yielded the intermediate E. The chiral
2-azetine product 3aa was then produced through β-elimination
of the phosphine. In the one-pot reaction procedure, Lewis acid
BF activated the carbonyl group of 3aa. Subsequently,
sequential reduction/rearrangement/ring-opening reaction
through Et SiH occurred to give the intermediate G, which was
hydrolysed to produce the allene product 4aa.

To gain further insight into the stereoselectivity of the
current reaction, we performed theoretical calculations. The
calculated free energy profiles were shown in Figure 2. The
conversion of substrate 2a into the intermediate D generated a
chiral center and a chiral axis, therefore four possible reaction
pathways were discussed for the reaction of 2a and the
intermediate A. The Re-S pathway (Figure 2, black) was
identified as the more favourable reaction pathway in view of its
relatively lower reaction energy barrier (7.87 kcal/mol) than the
other three competing pathways. This can be attributed to the
weaker steric hindrance in the transition state structure C-ts in

view of the co-presence of three strong H-bonds and shorter
C1···C2 distance (2.29 Å, Figure 2) compared to the 2.33 Å in
4C-ts with only one H-bond or 2.26 Å in 2C-ts with two H-
bonds. Consequently, this energetically favourable pathway
resulted in the intermediate D, which dictated the configuration
of the product 3aa, being consistent with the experimental
observation.

In conclusion, we have achieved asymmetric construction of
chiral 2-azetines and axially chiral tetrasubstituted allenes in
moderate to high yields with good to excellent stereoselectivities
through phosphine catalysis. Chiral phosphine-catalyzed [2+2]
annulation of sulfamate-derived cyclic imines with yne-enones
produced enantioenriched 2-azetine derivatives, which was
treated with Et SiH, BF ·Et O and H O through a one-pot
procedure to give axially chiral tetrasubstituted allenes. This
new application of yne-enones in phosphine catalysis will inspire
more exploration on yne-enones as a versatile acceptor for
phosphine-catalysed reactions.
